title: A Story of Halves
author: TextSavvy
summary: TextSavvy presents the second installment in a series building fractions from students' prior intuitions about wholes. The article's central argument is that mathematical concepts must be introduced through meaning and language before any procedural or symbolic representation — students should be able to talk about what they are counting before they are asked to calculate. The piece illustrates this by reframing the denominator as a unit-of-measure name: /2 means 'halves,' not 'divide into 2 equal parts,' a distinction that grounds fraction notation in intuition rather than algorithmic directives. The author argues that opening with procedural definitions strips mathematics of its 'about-ness,' producing students who can execute steps without understanding what they are measuring. A number-line tracing exercise demonstrates how the same physical movement can reveal both whole-number and fraction counting as parallel linguistic systems, allowing students to feel equivalence between, say, 1 whole and 2 halves before formalizing the relationship. The essay concludes by connecting this instructional approach to the author's longstanding design principles — precision, clarity, order, and cohesion — framed not as rules for textbooks but as criteria for the underlying story a teacher constructs for learners.
points: The denominator should be introduced as a linguistic name for a unit of measure (/2 = 'halves') before it is taught as a procedural directive ('divide into 2 equal parts'), because the procedural meaning changes across contexts while the naming convention remains stable.

Teaching procedure before meaning subtly bypasses the 'about-ness' of a concept — students learn to execute steps without understanding what they are measuring or counting, which undermines lasting comprehension.

Whole-number and fraction counting can be presented as parallel linguistic systems on a number line (0/1, 1/1, 2/1 vs. 0/2, 1/2, 2/2), allowing students to experience equivalence (1 whole = 2 halves) through movement before any formal rule is introduced.

Advocating for math as language is not a rejection of procedural fluency — it is a rejection of procedural understanding as a substitute for conceptual grounding, and practice remains central once meaning is established.

The instructional design principles of precision, clarity, order, and cohesion apply most powerfully to the underlying conceptual story a teacher tells, not just to textbook formatting or lesson sequencing.
quotes: the denominator '1' is the name for the unit of measure we call 'wholes' and the denominator '2' is the name for the unit of measure we call 'halves.' These names are presented as arbitrary because that's what they are: /2 indicates 'halves,' not 'think of this amount as having 2 equal parts.' The latter is a proceduralization (unpacking) of a meaning taught before the meaning itself.

we want students to see denominators as a kind of stable linguistic category that is intuitively extensible (after wholes and halves: thirds, fourths, fifths . . . ) before they turn them into numeric directives. Because those directives will change! In some stories, the directive will be to think of 2 equal parts; but in others, it will be "divide by 2.

Whenever I make the case for math to be taught "as a language," something like the above is what I mean—it should mean something to you before you write or draw something next. We should be talking about it first (if possible) in some way—up to the storyteller—that does not tacitly define it as a calculative command or require an externalization of thinking.
To start with a procedural definition of some mathematical concept is to subtly skip over the grounding 'about-ness' of the concept: what is this about? and how do we talk about it?

It is antagonistic to procedural understanding, not to procedural fluency, and it means (especially when we want concept before procedure) that students are supported well in their mathematical learning when they are able to know and talk about mathematics as a set of ideas that lead to certain procedures—not as a set of procedures.
The fractions that are at the same point, like 1 whole and 2 halves, are different ways of saying the same amount.

Each 'slide' across reinforces the continuousness of fraction 'measurement,' complementing our discrete models, and reveals new information each time, allowing for the body to feel the equivalence: the same trip shows 'wholes' one time, 'halves' another, and both together.
